summary:
Luxembourg's legal gender recognition framework rests on self-determination. The Act of 10 August 2018 replaced the previous long and costly judicial procedure with a declaration-based route to change gender status and first name(s) in the civil register, administered through the official government portal Guichet.lu. The procedure is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Recognition is binary; no nonbinary gender marker is available.

The reform was presented in May 2017 by Justice Minister Félix Braz as a bill allowing trans and intersex people to alter civil status by declaration, and it was welcomed by LGBTI associations at the time. The Chamber of Deputies approved the simplified procedure in July 2018.

Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited in employment, goods and services, education and health, with complaints handled by the CET equality body. Gender expression and sex characteristics are not named as protected grounds. The Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale provides services to LGBTI people in the country and documents this framework in its human-rights reporting.

A national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018. In July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, which organisations criticised for omitting depathologisation and other elements they consider essential.

As of 2019 reporting, Luxembourgian criminal law lacked aggravating circumstances for LGBTphobic assault, and under-reporting by victims was documented. The justice minister signalled that the law would evolve following the 2017 intervention of a European anti-discrimination monitoring body.

Prison policy is protective rather than punitive. The prison administration places detainees who disclose or openly show LGBT or trans identity so that they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations assessed case by case on the information gathered about the individual; such placements are described as exceptional. Requests by LGBT detainees to be housed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the Justice Ministry has warned against measures that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff additionally honour a detainee's chosen form of address. The planned Uerschterhaff prison at Sanem was designed with multiple sections allowing separation by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, within those, sexual orientation. Placement therefore follows disclosed identity and need with no codified birth-sex rule, no documented special custody unit, and no solitary or administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners.

Marriage and adoption are available to same-sex couples. The country has no measures addressing conversion practices, and no measures regulating intersex medical interventions.
tangentialFactors:
Luxembourg appears in both the LGBTQ+ Travel Safety Index and its companion Global Transgender Rights Index (Asher Fergusson, updated June 2023), which rank jurisdictions on laws affecting traveller safety; the country's placement in these commercial indexes rests on the same legal provisions set out above rather than on any incident record.

External review has driven part of the reform agenda. The 2017 intervention by a European anti-discrimination monitoring body preceded the justice ministry's commitment to revisit penalties for LGBTphobic assault, and Luxembourg's gender-recognition law was framed in the universal periodic review process by national civil-society submissions, including the UPR submission of the Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale in April 2023.

The 2025 action plan was published while LGBTI organisations were publicly pressing for depathologisation and for measures on conversion practices and intersex interventions, indicating that gaps remain between the national strategy and the demands of local service providers.
localsOnly:
Residents change gender status and first name(s) in the civil register through Guichet.lu by declaration, without judicial proceedings; the same route is available to resident foreign nationals.

Discrimination complaints in employment, goods and services, education and health are filed with the CET, and the Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale operates as a domestic service and advocacy organisation.

Detainees are entitled to be addressed by surname under a 1989 grand-ducal regulation, and staff additionally honour the chosen form of address; an LGBT or trans detainee's placement decision is taken case by case, and a request to enter an ordinary section is generally granted.

The Justice Ministry keeps no statistics on LGBT prisoners, on the basis that identifying them would require an unlawful interference with privacy.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2019 press report on the absence of LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances is the most recent hate-crime item in the available sources. Whether the promised aggravating circumstances were subsequently enacted is unresolved and not sourced here.

No source in the inventory documents a trans-specific violent incident in Luxembourg, its investigation, or its outcome; the violence picture rests on the under-reporting finding and on prison-placement policy rather than on case records.

The claim that no special custody unit or segregation practice exists for trans prisoners derives from a 2015 ministerial answer; whether this remains the case in the current prison estate, including the Uerschterhaff facility once opened, is not sourced.

Enforcement data for the discrimination prohibitions, including complaint volumes and outcomes before the CET, is not available in the inventory.
